questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Curve
questions.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$, can be found by computing $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j \\ ∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) & =2(-\frac{1}{2})\text{ }i+2(\frac{1}{2})\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})}{‖∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})‖} & =\frac{-i+j}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-i+j}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point  where $(x,y)=(1,1)$, can be found by computing $∇g(1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & ={g}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{g}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot y\,i+\frac{1}{xy}\cdot x\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j \\ ∇g(1,1) & =\frac{1}{(1)}\,i+\frac{1}{(1)}\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇g(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇g(1,1)}{‖∇g(1,1)‖} & =\frac{i+j}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(1,4)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,4).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y})\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,j \\ ∇f(1,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1}}\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{2}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,4)}{‖∇f(1,4)‖} & =\frac{\frac{1}{2}(i+j)}{‖\frac{1}{2}(i+j)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}})}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,0)$, can be found by computing $∇f(0,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y}+x+y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y}+x+y)\text{ }j \\  & =({e}^{x+y}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{x+y}+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,0) & =({e}^{0+0}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{0+0}+1)\text{ }j \\  & =2i+2j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(0,0)}{‖∇f(0,0)‖} & =\frac{2i+2j}{\sqrt{(2)^{2}+(2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2i+2j}{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=x+3y-2xy$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{3}{2},1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+3y-2xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+3y-2xy)\text{ }j \\  & =(1-2y)\text{ }i+(3-2x)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(\frac{3}{2},1) & =(1-2(1))\text{ }i+(3-2(\frac{3}{2}))\text{ }j \\  & =-i\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(\frac{3}{2},1):$

$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)=2xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =2xy \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y}-2y)\,i+(\frac{1}{x+y}-2x)\,j \\ ∇f(0,1) & =(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(0))\,j \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,1)=⟨-1,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1} & =\frac{y-1}{1} \\ -x & =y-1 \\ x+y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $2xy+6{y}^{2}=x-2.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(8,-3).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy+6{y}^{2} & =x-2 \\ 2xy+6{y}^{2}-x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2xy+6{y}^{2}-x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(8,-3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(8,-3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(8,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy+6{y}^{2}-x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+6{y}^{2}-x)\,j \\  & =(2y-1)\,i+(2x+12y)\,j \\ ∇f(8,-3) & =(2(-3)-1)\,i+(2(8)+12(-3))\,j \\  & =-7\,i-20\,j \\  & =⟨-7,-20⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 Hence, $∇f(8,-3)=⟨-7,-20⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(8,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-8}{-7} & =\frac{y-(-3)}{-20} \\ -20(x-8) & =-7(y+3) \\ -20x+7y+160+21 & =0 \\ -20x+7y+181 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $6xy=5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy & =5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy)\,j \\  & =(10x-6y)\,i+(2y-6x)\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(10-6(1))\,i+(2(1)-6)\,j \\  & =4\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨4,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,1)=⟨4,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{4} & =\frac{y-1}{-4} \\ x-1 & =-y+1 \\ x+y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the plane curve $\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=2y-x-2.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =2y-x-2 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+1)i+(\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-2)j \\ ∇f(0,2) & =(\frac{0}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}}+1)i+(\frac{2}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}}-2)j \\  & =i-j \\  & =⟨1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,2)=⟨1,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,2).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-2}{-1} \\ x & =2-y \\ x+y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=4.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =2(2)\,i+2(0)\,j \\  & =4\,i \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨4,0⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-2)0-(y-0)4 & =0 \\ -4y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(3,4,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,k \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(3,4,0) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,i+\frac{4}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,j+\frac{0}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $3{x}^{2}-xz=6-3xyz$ at the point $(1,0,-3).$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-xz & =6-3xyz \\ 3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz & =6\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=6.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,-3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,-3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz)k \\  & =(6x-z+3yz)\text{ }i+3xz\text{ }j+(-x+3xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,-3) & =(6(1)-(-3)+3(0)(-3))\text{ }i+3(1)(-3)\text{ }j+(-1+3(1)(0))\text{ }k \\  & =9\,i-9\,j-k \\  & =⟨9,-9,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{9}=\frac{y-0}{-9}=\frac{z-(-3)}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{9}=\frac{y}{-9}=\frac{z+3}{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}yz=-4$ at the point $(2,-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}yz.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-4.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(2,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}yz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}yz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}yz)k \\  & =2xyz\text{ }i+{x}^{2}z\text{ }j+{x}^{2}y\,k \\ ∇f(2,-1,1) & =2(2)(-1)(1)\text{ }i+(2)^{2}(1)\text{ }j+(2)^{2}(-1)\text{ }k \\  & =-4\,i+4\,j-4\,k \\  & =⟨-4,4,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-2}{(-4)}=\frac{y-(-1)}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-4)} \\ \frac{x-2}{(-1)}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-1}{(-1)} \\ 2-x=y+1=1-z\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}z+y-\frac{\pi }{2}$ at the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y) & ={x}^{2}z+y-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ {z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)k \\  & =(2xy{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-2xz)i+({x}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-1)j+(2z\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2})k \\ ∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =(2(-1)(\frac{\pi }{2})(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-2(-1)(1))i+((-1)^{2}(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-1)j+(2(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-(-1)^{2})k \\  & =(-\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+2)i+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-1)j+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-1)k \\  & =2\,i-j+k \\  & =⟨2,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ and passes through the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1⟩+t\,∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)=⟨-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1⟩+t\,⟨2,-1,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

questions.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x=5$ at the point $(1,-1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=5.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)k \\  & =(2xy+{z}^{2})\,i+({x}^{2}+2yz)\,j+({y}^{2}+2zx)\,k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(2(1)(-1)+(2)^{2})\text{ }i+((1)^{2}+2(-1)(2))\text{ }j+((-1)^{2}+2(2)(1))\text{ }k \\  & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k \\  & =⟨2,-3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,-1,2)$ and passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,∇f(1,-1,2)=⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,⟨2,-3,5⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

canonical_examples.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y) = x^2 + 2y^2 +x$ that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1, 1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,1).$  

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,j \\  & =(2x+0+1)\,i+(0+4y+0)\,j \\  & =(2x+1)\,i+4y\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(2(1)+1)\,i+4(1)\,j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we want a unit normal vector, we normalize $\nabla f(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,1)}{‖∇f(1,1)‖} & =\frac{3\,i+4\,j}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the plane curve $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0, 4).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16} - 1,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(0,4).$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)j \\  & =\frac{2x}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{8}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{(4)}{8}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j \\  & =⟨0,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{x-{x}_{0}}=\frac{{v}_{y}}{{v}_{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{y}(x-{x}_{0}) & ={v}_{x}(y-{y}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(x-0) & =0(y-4) \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that the equation of the normal line to the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1$ at the point $(0,4)$ is $x=0.$

canonical_examples.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z) = 2x^2 - xy - z^2,$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)$ can be found by computing 
$\nabla f(2, 3, \sqrt 2).$   

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }k \\  & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j-2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,3,\sqrt{2}) & =(4\cdot 2-3)\text{ }i-2\text{ }j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k \\  & =5i-2j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $5 \mathbf i  - 2 \mathbf j - 2 \sqrt 2\ \mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z = \ln (x^2 - xy)$ at the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z) = \ln (x^2 - xy) - z,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2){:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)k \\  & =(\frac{2x-y}{{x}^{2}-xy})\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{y-x})\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =(\frac{2\cdot 2-1}{{2}^{2}-2\cdot 1})\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{1-2})\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{3}{2}i-\,j-k \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf v = \langle v_x, v_y, v_z \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2)= \left\langle  \dfrac {3} {2}, -1, -1\right  \rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})}=\frac{y-1}{-1}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-1} \\ \frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$
